text.p: These are the leading stories in the Belgrade press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified them and does not vouch for their accuracy.
NASA BORBA
- Teachers protest outside Serbian government for tenth day demanding higher and timely pay. Some schools resume classes after strike of more than one month.
- London expresses full support for democratisation of Serbia during Zajedno (Together) coalition leaders' visit to Britain.
- Montenegrin Prime Minister Milo Djukanovic to visit Washington soon. According to some sources, Montenegro is preparing the ground to independently join international financial institutions.
- One percent of turnover tax on all products should be set aside to finance agriculture, says Rajko Vulovic of the chamber of commerce of Vojvodina province, Yugoslavia's breadbasket.
- Drop in January Serbian budget income to 672 million dinars from 1.14 billion in December. Fall in wages main reason for depleted budget and pension and health funds.
- Montenegro development fund expects total investment potential in 1997 to be at least 25 million dinars.
- Serbian Information Minister Radmila Milentijevic says draft law on information will be sent to all political parties and registered media prior to adoption in a few weeks.

- Opposition parties and humanitarian organisations accuse Serbian and Montenegrin authorities of silence on the case of 19 train passengers who were kidnapped four years ago. The Moslems from Montenegro, on a Belgrade-Bar train, were kidnapped in Strpci, Bosnia.
- Serbian Chamber of Commerce President Vlajko Stojiljkovic calls on federal government to explain "unreasonable imports" of 180,000 tonnes of sugar last year.
POLITIKA
- Credit arrangement with pharmaceutical companies ICN Galenika and Velefarma Belgrade to regulate supply of medicines which are in short supply on the market.
- Vojislav Tomic of the central bank treasury department says National Bank of Yugoslavia denies rumours that 500 and 1,000 dinar bills will soon be printed.

- Both Dafiment and Jugoskandik banks, two pyramid investment schemes that collapsed in 1994, operated with central bank permits. There is hope for hard currency savings accounts holders whose funds were frozen in 1991.
- Serbian Agriculture Minister Jovan Babovic says spring sowing and repayment of debt to farmers are priority tasks.
- Privatisation a priority, Bosnian Serb Republic and Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina economic experts agree at joint meeting in Banja Luka.

- International aid to former Yugoslav republics to be reduced by 30-50 percent this year compared to 1996 but needs unchanged, participants at meeting of international and Yugoslav red cross organisations say.
VECERNJE NOVOSTI

- Yugoslavia's return to the International Monetary Fund and World Bank further away again. On list of 135 high-risk countries for investment, Yugoslavia in 129th place. Some firms forced to accept humiliating conditions offered by foreign companies to keep operating. -- Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
